text: TCP and UDP are the two workhorse transport-layer protocols, and they make opposite promises. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. UDP is connectionless and fast. Before any TCP data flows, both hosts perform a three-way handshake — and that handshake is exactly what makes TCP's reliability possible.

The client sends a SYN segment with a starting sequence number. The server replies with SYN-ACK — its own sequence number, plus an acknowledgment of the client's. The client sends a final ACK. Three segments, and now both sides agree the connection is open and know exactly where to start counting bytes.

SYN says, I'd like to talk, here's where my byte count starts. SYN-ACK says, I hear you, I'm listening, here's mine. ACK closes the loop. Only after all three does real application data start flowing — a web page, an email, a file.

TCP tracks every byte with a sequence number, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits anything lost, and reorders segments that arrive out of sequence — all invisible to the application sitting on top of it. UDP skips all of that entirely. It's connectionless, fire-and-forget: send the datagram and move on, with no handshake, no sequence numbers, and no guarantee it ever arrives at all.

That tradeoff decides which protocols use which transport. TCP carries HTTP and HTTPS web traffic, SMTP email, and FTP file transfers, because a missing byte would corrupt the result. UDP carries DNS queries — small enough that a lost one just gets retried — along with streaming video and VoIP, where a dropped packet is a minor glitch and not worth the delay of retransmission.

Loading a secure webpage means a TCP handshake on port 443 before a single byte of the page arrives, because every byte of that page has to show up intact and in order. A DNS lookup is one UDP packet on port 53, gone and answered in an instant, with the client just asking again if nothing comes back. Next up: the common ports every analyst needs memorized cold.
